extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and scientists interested in history/philosophy of science and literary criticism (readers of Popular Science Monthly)
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic critique comparing scientific and poetic approaches to color theory (Goethe vs Newton), extracting standards for good scientific practice, experiment, and argumentation. Useful for writing or evaluating critical essays about scientific theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of ocular demonstration and empirical fact
rubrics_metrics.description: "Newton's theory of colors, it may be remarked, is really less a 'theory' than a direct presentation of facts... The demonstration is ocular and complete. Having palpably decomposed the white light into its constituent colors, Newton recompounded these colors to white light. Both the analysis and the synthesis are matters of fact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations grounded in direct, reproducible observation and demonstration (analysis and synthesis). A scientific claim should be supported by experiments that make the phenomenon manifest to the senses (or instrumentation) and by re-composition/replication showing the causal link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and controlled complexity in experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton's 'pedantic accuracy' and apparently needless complications are defended as essential to the purity of experiments; Goethe regarded such complication as torturing the light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with the necessary complexity and controls even if they seem pedantic; thorough, carefully controlled procedures can be essential to reveal subtle physical effects. Do not avoid methodological rigor for the sake of simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and clear logical force of experimental results
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe repeated Newton's experiments and 'in almost every case obtained his results' but was criticized for finding them incomplete and lacking logical force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not only must experiments be repeatable, but their interpretation must be logically compelling. Report conditions precisely (setups, distances, measurements) and show how results lead to the claimed inference rather than relying on impressionistic readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, ad hoc explanatory devices (e.g., 'turbid media')
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe's appeal to 'turbid media' to explain diverse phenomena is criticized as entangling him in poor physical theory: 'His turbid media entangle him everywhere, leading him captive and committing him to almost incredible delusions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor mechanistic, physically plausible explanations over vague catch-all constructs. If introducing a novel explanatory concept, define it precisely and show how it yields testable predictions across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep scientific argument distinct from personal invective or ethical judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe, in 'unmasking' Newton, 'delivers himself over to the guidance of his emotions' and levels moral accusations; the essay warns that mixing subject and object is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique theories by addressing evidence and reasoning; avoid ad hominem attacks, moralizing about an opponent's character, or extended invective which undermines the rhetorical force of valid criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and state the limits of experiments and avoid overgeneralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe asserted 'by experiment nothing can really be proved... Phenomena may be observed and classified; experiments may be accurately executed, and made thus to represent a certain circle of human knowledge,' implying limits to what an experiment can establish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the scope and limits of your experimental findings. Avoid extrapolating beyond the domain the experiment is designed to probe; qualify conclusions appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use methods appropriate to the discipline; do not import unsuitable approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe is criticized for attempting 'to ingraft in his "Farbenlehre" methods altogether foreign to physics on to the treatment of a purely physical theme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conceptual and methodological tools suited to the subject (e.g., physical, mathematical methods for physics problems). Where cross-disciplinary methods are used, justify their applicability and adapt them carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of originality and independent critical thinking over mere repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay disparages Newton's imitators: 'To take up the error of another, and persist in it with stiff-necked obstinacy, is a proof of poor qualities... the stupidity of the copyist irritates and renders us miserable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work for independent thinking and willingness to question received opinion; avoid mindless repetition of established doctrines without scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clarity and convincing demonstration over spectacle or quantity of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe accuses Newton of heaping 'experiment on experiment, fiction upon fiction, seeking to dazzle where he cannot convince' — the essay notes that experiments should convince rather than merely overwhelm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for experiments that make the argument clear and convincing; a large number of experiments is not a substitute for well-designed, interpretable demonstrations. Present the simplest decisive tests where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate ethical/psychological interpretation from empirical evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe attempts to explain Newton's theory by examining 'Newton's Persönlichkeit' (his character), an approach the essay criticizes: 'we are not at liberty to mix together subject and object as Goethe mixed himself with Newton.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explaining scientific errors primarily by imputing moral failings or psychological motives to the scientist; instead, focus on methodological, theoretical, or evidential causes for mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge objective truth and guard against individual prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay states: 'In science there exists, apart from the individual, objective truth; and the fate of Goethe's own theory... illustrates how, in the progress of humanity, the individual, if he err, is left stranded and forgotten.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims against independent empirical standards rather than personal sympathies or prejudices. Emphasize community-verifiable evidence as the arbiter of scientific truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate tolerance between disciplinary modes (science and poetry) while respecting their differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay argues that 'poetry is an element just as much as science' and that 'there is no necessary encroachment of the one field upon the other... Nature embraces them both.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing or integrating insights across disciplines, respect the distinct aims and methods of each. Encourage interdisciplinary dialogue but avoid expecting one mode (e.g., poetic intuition) to substitute for another (e.g., experimental proof).
